title: Connected Speech: Linking R, Intrusive R, T-Flapping & H-Dropping
objectives: Produce linking and intrusive R across word boundaries
Apply American T-flapping (/d/ sound) between vowels
Recognize informal H-dropping in function words

teacherNotes.title: Anticipated Problems & Solutions (CELTA Standard)
teacherNotes.content:
⚠️ Problem: Learner speaks word-by-word with choppy pauses.
💡 Solution: Drill 2-word phrases as single units: far-away, tell-him, water.

elements.content: Gabarit 14 Champs: Connected Speech: Linking R, Intrusive R, T-Flapping & H-Dropping
1. Definition: Phonological processes that smooth transitions between words in natural fluent speech.

2. Rule: 1. Linking R: Pronounce final silent R before a vowel (far away -> /fɑːr əˈweɪ/). 2. Intrusive R: Insert /r/ between final vowel /ɔː, ɑː, ə/ and initial vowel (law and order -> /lɔːr ən ˈɔːrdər/). 3. T-Flapping (US): Intervocalic /t/ becomes quick tap [ɾ]/[d] (water -> /wɔːtər/ -> [wɔːdər]). 4. H-Dropping: Unstressed "he, him, her, have" drop h (tell him -> /tɛl ɪm/).
3. Why? Maximizes articulatory economy and flow across speech boundaries.
4. How to recognize? Word boundary environments in natural connected speech.
5. Common examples: far away /fɑːr əˈweɪ/, law and order /lɔːr ən ˈɔːrdər/, water /ˈwɔːtər/, better /ˈbɛtər/, tell him /tɛl ɪm/, cup of coffee /kʌp əv ˈkɔːfi/
6. Counter-examples: Formal citation style or distinct emphatic pauses between words.
7. Exceptions: H is never dropped when stressed at sentence start (He arrived).
8. Common mistakes: Inserting glottal stops between vowels instead of linking smoothly.
9. Mnemonic / Hint: Fluid speech connects words! Water = "wadder", tell him = "tell-im"!
10. Key vocabulary: connected speech, linking R, intrusive R, T-flapping, H-dropping, assimilation
11. Frequency: ★★★★★ (Essential)
12. CEFR Level: 🔵 B2
13. Associated Visual: 🔗 Chain link joining two words together in fluent speech.
14. Key Takeaway: Connected speech glues words together smoothly!

teacherNotes.title: Teacher CCQ Script
teacherNotes.content: Ask these concept checking questions to verify rule understanding without translation:

elements.content: Rule Understanding Check (CCQ):
CCQ 1: What sound connects "far" and "away" in fluent speech? (/r/ linking sound)
CCQ 2: How is the "t" in "water" pronounced in American English? (As a quick tap /d/ sound)
CCQ 3: What happens to the "h" in "tell him" in fast natural speech? (It drops: "tell-im")

teacherNotes.title: Stage aim
teacherNotes.content: Auditory discrimination, minimal pairs, and guided oral drill repetition.
